Name: prereasoning_budget_direction
Title: The Budget Is Set Before Thinking Begins: Reading and Steering a Pre-Reasoning Compute-Allocation Direction for Efficient Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models form an internal estimate of how much thinking a problem 'deserves' in the residual stream at the prompt-processing stage, before any reasoning token is generated. This pre-reasoning compute-budget estimate is linearly decodable and causally controls eventual CoT length. It is systematically miscalibrated (over-budgeting on easy items). Reading it enables per-instance budget forecasting, and steering it along a single 'budget direction' can recalibrate thinking length at its source—cutting tokens with minimal accuracy loss—more cheaply and interpretably than mid-chain sufficiency probes or truncation.
Related Work: Mid-chain approaches probe whether the generated prefix is sufficient (BLADE), whether generation will converge within budget (Token Budget Saturation), or route tokens by entropy (R-Stitch), and adaptive-depth methods (System-1.5) allocate compute per token during generation. Steering methods (SEAL, CATS, ACTS) modify hidden states or issue strategies during reasoning. All of these operate DURING reasoning. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) we identify a compute-budget representation that exists at the PROMPT stage before the first reasoning token, characterizing when the die is cast; (2) we show this pre-reasoning estimate causally determines and is miscalibrated relative to the actual difficulty; (3) we recalibrate at the source via a single interpretable steering direction applied once at prompt time, rather than repeated mid-chain interventions or truncation. This bridges interpretability (where does overthinking originate?) with a minimal, single-shot efficiency intervention.
Abstract: Efficient-reasoning methods overwhelmingly intervene during chain-of-thought (CoT) generation—probing sufficiency, forecasting convergence, or steering mid-trace. We ask a prior question: is a model's thinking budget already decided before it emits a single reasoning token? We hypothesize that during prompt processing, reasoning models encode a latent compute-budget estimate in the residual stream that (a) is linearly decodable, (b) predicts the eventual CoT length, and (c) causally controls how long the model thinks. We first train lightweight linear probes on final-prompt-token hidden states to predict eventual CoT length, and measure how early and how accurately budget is forecastable. We then extract a 'budget direction' via difference-of-means between prompts yielding long vs. short traces, and use causal activation steering—applied once at the prompt position—to lengthen or shorten reasoning, confirming causality with dose-response curves. Crucially, by comparing the model's internal budget estimate against a difficulty oracle (per-item pass rate), we quantify systematic over-budgeting on easy problems, offering a mechanistic account of overthinking as a prompt-stage miscalibration. Finally, we build a training-free controller that (i) reads the budget probe to forecast, then (ii) applies calibrated negative-direction steering only when the model over-budgets, recalibrating thinking length at its source. We evaluate accuracy-vs-tokens Pareto curves on GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA across DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-8B, against truncation, entropy early-exit, and BLADE/ACTS-style baselines, expecting 20-40% token savings at near-equal accuracy with a single interpretable intervention.
Experiments: 1. Budget forecastability: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-8B, generate full CoT on GSM8K, MATH, ProntoQA. Record eventual CoT length (tokens until answer). Train linear/ridge probes on hidden states at the final prompt token (across layers) to predict log CoT length. Report R^2 and how it varies by layer; compare to a probe using only the first K reasoning tokens to show budget is largely set before reasoning. 2. Causal validation: Extract a 'budget direction' via difference-of-means between prompt-token hidden states of long-trace vs. short-trace instances (matched for correctness). Add/subtract scaled multiples of this direction at the final prompt position and measure resulting CoT length: expect monotonic dose-response. Controls: random directions, orthogonalized directions, other-layer directions. 3. Miscalibration analysis: Estimate per-item difficulty via pass@k / self-consistency accuracy. Correlate internal budget estimate (probe output) with realized length and with difficulty; identify 'over-budgeting' items where budget >> difficulty warrants. Quantify the fraction of total tokens attributable to over-budgeting. 4. Source-recalibration controller (training-free): For each prompt, read the budget probe; if predicted budget exceeds a difficulty-calibrated threshold, apply negative-direction steering at the prompt position with strength calibrated by the excess. Generate normally afterward with NO further intervention. 5. Evaluation: accuracy vs. mean tokens generated (Pareto), wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, fixed truncation, entropy/confidence early-exit, and reproductions of BLADE-style mid-chain sufficiency exit and ACTS-style steering. Metrics: accuracy, tokens, probe R^2, steering dose-response slope, fraction of items recalibrated. 6. Ablations: layer choice for direction, steering position (prompt vs. first-reasoning-token), cross-dataset and cross-model transfer of the budget direction/probe, per-difficulty accuracy breakdown to confirm savings come from easy items.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Budget may only be weakly forecastable at the prompt stage for hard/ambiguous items, limiting how much of thinking is 'pre-decided'; the layer/early-probe analysis quantifies this and defines the method's scope. 2. Steering at the prompt position could degrade problem understanding rather than just shortening thinking; dose-response controls and accuracy tracking guard against this, and we cap steering strength. 3. The budget direction may entangle difficulty with surface features (prompt length, topic); we control by matching for correctness and testing orthogonalized directions. 4. Difficulty oracle via pass@k is compute-intensive offline but only needed for calibration, not at inference. 5. Direction/probe may not transfer across models, requiring cheap per-model calibration done once; transfer is tested explicitly. 6. Aggressive recalibration risks hurting the hardest items—Pareto and per-difficulty analyses make this trade-off explicit.
